extracted.intended_audience: scholars and journal editors considering or running adversarial collaborations (primarily social and behavioral scientists)
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and executing adversarial collaborations (ACs) — collaborative studies in which investigators with competing models jointly design, analyze, and interpret research to test competing predictions. Includes practical steps for team formation, design, conflict management, documentation, and publication strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carefully choose adversaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Carefully choose adversaries; not everyone is suited for these projects. Ideal collaborators have intellectual humility, a respectful approach to others’ ideas, a willingness to learn from adversaries, and are genuinely open and curious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participants emphasized selecting people with the right temperament and disposition. Advice includes being selective about who to work with and prioritizing collaborators who will engage respectfully and constructively. Anti-patterns: recruiting individuals who are combative, unwilling to compromise, or overly invested in prior positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Involve a neutral third-party arbiter
rubrics_metrics.description: Involve a neutral arbiter trusted and respected by both parties to help settle design disputes and maintain fairness throughout the process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arbiters mitigate conflict, maintain momentum, push collaborators toward deadlines, and can adopt tactics like pausing meetings, splitting collaborators into separate threads, or blinding themselves to conditions when conducting analyses. They should be impartial and able to creatively resolve disputes. Example: an arbiter blinded herself to conditions before analyses to avoid partiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep extensive documentation and pre-project agreements
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep thorough, transparent documentation throughout the project, including pre-project agreements that function 'almost as a contract' to hold collaborators accountable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documentation should include clearly articulated methods, agreed-upon protocols, and records of decisions. This supports accountability, reduces post-hoc disputes, and aligns with open science norms. Anti-patterns: vague agreements or lack of written protocols that allow parties to reinterpret decisions later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-register methodology and pre-specify analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: The methodology must be well pre-registered beforehand; pre-specify design and analysis decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-registration helps constrain analytic flexibility and motivated reasoning. The authors recommend combining ACs with registered reports (RRs) so studies are evaluated on methods prior to data collection, protecting nuanced AC results from being penalized in peer review. Scoring note: stronger pre-registration and specificity increases credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Involve early-career scholars
rubrics_metrics.description: Involve individuals at different career stages; junior researchers are often less committed to existing theories and can help resolve conflicts and analyze data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Senior scholars provide representation and expertise; junior scholars contribute flexibility and may be less tied to prior positions. Use team composition intentionally to balance incentives and openness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select questions suited to ACs (well-defined, discriminative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose appropriate questions: ACs work best when there is a genuine, well-defined disagreement and when an experimental design can discriminate between competing hypotheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participants noted ACs should target disputes where design decisions can be jointly agreed to discriminate theories. Anti-patterns: applying ACs to ill-posed or overly broad disputes where no single experiment can distinguish sides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect and plan for greater upfront effort and time
rubrics_metrics.description: ACs are more challenging and require more upfront effort than typical projects, often because of lengthy discussions around operational definitions and methodological choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan for extended design negotiations and coordination costs; however, upfront investment can save time during peer review and improve post-publication debate. Project timelines and resource allocation should reflect higher initial effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate nuanced results rather than decisive winners
rubrics_metrics.description: ACs tend not to produce a clear 'winner' but instead produce a deeper, more nuanced understanding of the problem space and boundary conditions where different theories hold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set expectations for subtle, context-dependent findings rather than dramatic single-study victories. Consider how this affects reporting, claims, and likely reception in peer review (may favor registered reports or journals that value rigor over novelty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiverse approaches and pretesting
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ multiverse analysis and frequent pretesting of materials to explore multiple analysis choices and contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiverse methods expose how different reasonable analytic choices affect results and reduce the chance that a single analytic path drives conclusions. Pretesting materials helps ensure operationalizations are fair and robust across perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain an interpersonal culture of respect and openness
rubrics_metrics.description: Foster an interpersonal culture where participants focus on their own behavior, treat adversaries well, and encourage respect and openness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arbiters and collaborators advised focusing on conduct: treating adversaries well tends to elicit reciprocation. Building norms of respect, curiosity, and openness reduces conflict and supports productive negotiation. Anti-patterns: adversarial personal attacks, rhetorical victory-seeking, or focusing on 'winning' rather than understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use arbiters proactively to manage process (conflict and momentum)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arbiters should proactively manage conflict and momentum: pause heated meetings, split communications if necessary, push collaborators to meet deadlines, and devise creative process rules (e.g., blinding) to preserve fairness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalize arbiter responsibilities in the project plan. Effective arbiters both defuse interpersonal tensions and keep the project progressing. Example tactics: temporary pauses, separate negotiation threads, arbiter-conducted blinded analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt open science practices beyond preregistration (data sharing, transparency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow open science norms—preregistration, data sharing, collaborative research practices, and transparent reporting—to improve reproducibility and clarity of ACs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open practices complement AC aims by making choices and data available for scrutiny. This helps address motivated reasoning and supports post-publication debate. Anti-patterns: opacity in methods or data that undermines trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document prior beliefs, methods, and implications to promote accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Extensively document beliefs, methods, and their implications before conducting studies to make it harder for collaborators to cling to positions when evidence contradicts them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-study documentation of theoretical priors and expected patterns increases accountability and makes post-hoc rationalization more visible. This can be integrated into pre-registration or supplemental materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider alternative team recruitment strategies when primary proponents opt out
rubrics_metrics.description: If primary proponents are unwilling to participate, recruit peripheral collaborators of proponents rather than main proponents to allow perspectives to converge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This tactic may allow relevant perspectives to be represented even when primary adversaries decline; however, it risks not fully representing maximal disagreement. Use transparently and document rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote systemic support (journal/organization roles) for ACs
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals and organizations could implement standardized methods for identifying conflicts and assembling AC teams to scale and broaden adoption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors propose that systematic approaches (e.g., editorial initiatives, support for registered reports of ACs) could expand ACs' reach, help resolve disputes, and regain trust in rigorous methods. Implementation guidance: editorial policies, curated matchmaking, or funding support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor prediction-focused or solution-oriented ACs for societal impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate prediction tasks or focus on solution-oriented problems where findings have practical implications to increase the value and societal impact of ACs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Projects with real-world applications (policy-relevant or solution-oriented) may better integrate adversarial perspectives and enhance both scientific rigor and societal relevance. Example references: Hofman et al. (prediction), Watts (solution-oriented).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limits: ACs are not universally scalable or suitable
rubrics_metrics.description: ACs have limited scalability and are not suited to all scholars or topics; they work best with the right temperament and well-defined disputes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat ACs as a targeted tool rather than a universal method. Consider costs (slower tempo, greater coordination) and weigh trade-offs between depth/rigor and pace of research.
